title: Choroidal Rupture: Trauma, Tears, and the Threat of CNVM
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the mechanical disruption of the RPE-Bruch's-Choroid complex following blunt ocular trauma. Focuses on diagnosis, multimodal imaging, and the high-stakes management of secondary CNVM.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Choroidal rupture is a linear or crescent-shaped tear involving the choroid, Bruch's membrane, and the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE). It occurs following blunt ocular trauma when the elastic sclera withstands the impact while the less elastic inner layers (Bruch's/RPE) undergo mechanical failure.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Kinetic Chain
content: 1. High-velocity blunt impact to the anterior globe.
2. Rapid anteroposterior compression of the globe.
3. Compensatory equatorial expansion and stretching of posterior coats.
4. Tensile strength of Bruch's membrane is exceeded (least elastic layer).
5. Mechanical rupture of RPE, Bruch's, and Choriocapillaris.
6. Immediate hemorrhage into sub-RPE or subretinal spaces.

rows: At the site of impact (usually anterior)
High risk of central vision loss (macular)

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Acute Phase: Obscured by subretinal/vitreous hemorrhage.
Early Sign: Commotio retinae (Berlin's Edema) in surrounding area.
Late Phase: Yellowish-white crescentic streak (sclera showing through).
Location: Usually temporal to the optic disc.
Associated: Peripapillary pigmentary changes.
Margins: Well-demarcated with Pigmentary hyperplasia at edges.

rows: Disruption of the RPE/Bruch's complex; 'step-off' appearance; detects secondary CNVM.
Early: Hypofluorescence (masking by blood); Late: Staining of the scar or leakage if CNVM.
Better visualization through hemorrhage; shows hypofluorescent dark lines.
Hypo-autofluorescence at the site of the rupture (RPE loss).
Indicated if vitreous hemorrhage prevents fundus view; check for RD.

sections.title: Delayed Complication: Traumatic CNVM
content: Occurs in 5-25% of patients.
Typically develops 6 months to 5 years after injury.
Higher risk if the rupture is close to the foveal center.
Sudden metamorphopsia or central scotoma is a 'Red Flag'.
Requires immediate OCT/FA to confirm neovascularization.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Immediate Post-Trauma: Bed rest, head elevation (if active bleeding).
2. Observation: Monthly follow-up for 6 months, then Q3-6 months.
3. Home Monitoring: Daily Amsler Grid is mandatory for the patient.
4. Active CNVM: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, or Bevacizumab).
5. Submacular Hemorrhage: Consider subretinal tPA and gas displacement if thick blood under fovea.

sections.title: Anti-VEGF Dosing for Traumatic CNVM
content: Standard: Bevacizumab (1.25mg) or Aflibercept (2.0mg).
Regimen: Pro Re Nata (PRN) or Treat-and-Extend.
Note: Often requires fewer injections than AMD-related CNVM.
Prognosis: Generally good response in younger patients.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques: Submacular Blood
content: 1. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV).
2. Injection of subretinal tPA (25 micrograms/0.1ml).
3. Fluid-Air exchange.
4. Intravitreal C3F8 or SF6 gas tamponade.
5. Strict prone positioning for 24-48 hours to displace blood.

sections.title: Mnemonic: The '4 C's' of Choroidal Rupture

content.explanation: Contusion (the cause), Crescent (the shape), Concentric (to the disc), CNVM (the complication).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The distance of the rupture from the fovea is the strongest predictor of CNVM risk.
Multiple ruptures carry a higher risk of CNVM than a single rupture.
Always check for associated trauma: Scleral rupture, RD, Angle recession (gonioscopy later), and Commotio.
Laser photocoagulation is now rarely used for CNVM due to scar expansion (foveal creep).

rows: Found that CNVM distance <1500 microns from fovea significantly increases vision loss risk.
Classified indirect ruptures and described the crescentic pattern concentric to the disc.
Demonstrated excellent visual outcomes in traumatic CNVM using Anti-VEGF monotherapy.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
content: Foveal Involvement: Guarded prognosis (20/200 or worse).
Extrafoveal Rupture: Excellent prognosis (20/40 or better).
Anti-VEGF Success: 70-80% achieve stabilization or improvement.
Long-term: Risk of 'foveal creep' where the atrophic scar expands toward the macula over decades.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Immediate Red Flags
content: Sudden drop in vision after initial stabilization.
New onset metamorphopsia (distorted lines).
Subretinal fluid or new hemorrhage on OCT.
Associated Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) - check for Optic Neuropathy.
